topics.topic: A21 security-review status after the A19 change
questions: Has the changed A19 been re-reviewed under every A21 category that references it, or is A21 currently reopened?
Has the revised A19 been reviewed and accepted under the injection category, or is A21 currently reopened and incomplete?
Has the changed A19 been re-reviewed so A21 may remain performed, or is A21 now reopened pending a new injection review?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about A21's status after A19, already judged answered.

precedent.topic: Security-review status and coverage after the A19 injection-rule change
quotes: A change to a decision a category names reopens this review.
Every decision a category names is accepted.
Security review: PERFORMED
- injection_interpreted_input: APPLICABLE; references: A02, A16, A19; affected: M03, M08, import file, every stored text value
- browser_boundary: APPLICABLE; references: A13, A19; affected: owner interface, CSRF protection, session cookie, rendering of agent-written text
precedent.why: The current performed and accepted A21 review expressly includes A19 in both affected categories, and the text supplies no later A19 change that would reopen it.

topics.topic: Algorithm and byte representation for import-file digests
questions: Which collision-resistant algorithm is used, and is the digest over the exact uploaded bytes or over a canonical parsed representation?
How is the import-file digest computed so every release binds and recognizes the same file without collision-prone or representation-dependent guesses?
Which digest algorithm and byte representation identify and bind an uploaded import file?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the import digest algorithm and byte representation, already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Import-file digest algorithm and canonical byte representation
quotes: The mapping names the file by its digest.
What Registry defines is the file it accepts on import; its format belongs to States 5 and 6.
precedent.why: The digest algorithm, canonical byte representation and encoded digest form are format and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Authenticated backup-encryption format and key handling
questions: What exact cryptographic construction makes a backup confidential and detects tampering or use of the wrong key?
What cryptographic format must every release use, and which readable metadata is authenticated, so a backup is confidential and tampering is detected consistently?
What authenticated-encryption and key-handling rules must every backend use for backups?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the authenticated backup-encryption format and key handling, already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Authenticated backup encryption format and authentication-failure handling
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Effect of failed pre-import backup deletion after closure backup verification
questions: Does the M10 condition become true when the post-import backup passes its check or only after every pre-import backup has actually been deleted?
When deletion of a pre-import backup fails after a closure-bearing backup passes its check, is that old backup still allowed to remain kept, and does the import remain accepted?
If deletion of a pre-import backup fails after the closure backup passes, may that old backup remain until a later run, or must Registry stop serving or otherwise ensure it is no longer kept?

quotes:
None; absent, then present forever: once a backup holding it has passed its
check, no backup without it is kept (State 2 A16, A18).

Once a backup holding the closure has passed its
   check, Registry deletes every backup made before the import, so no kept
   backup can bring back a store without the closure (M10). Until then a
   failed run is retried at the next run; the import stays accepted.

A backup or a deletion that fails leaves no partial file, writes a
   diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at
   the next run; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.why: M10 says no closure-free backup remains once the closure backup passes, while A18 permits a failed deletion to leave such a backup until a later run while Registry continues serving.

topics.topic: Restrictions and completion evidence during post-restore reconciliation
questions: What prevents service tokens from being configured and Registry restarted before the required reconciliation is complete?

May the backup scheduler copy the unreconciled restored store, thereby creating a fresh backup containing data that should already be erased, or must backups remain suspended until reconciliation is completed?
What prevents service tokens from being enabled before the required post-restore reconciliation is complete, and what evidence marks completion?

quotes:
A run that 03:00 found Registry stopped is made when
   it next starts, if no backup was made that UTC day; besides the run after
   an accepted import (A16), there is at most one run per UTC day, and runs
   never overlap.

The owner first starts the restored instance owner-only (A17 rule 1), so
   no service and no agent reaches it, and brings each Customer and project to
   the state the owner's own record of the retention review (R0-60) gives for
   it now — erased, restricted, ended or not — and erases audit entries before
   the latest date the owner erased by, before configuring the tokens and
   starting it again.

This is the owner's operation (Explicit exclusions: the
   host's administration), and the owner's record is its evidence; Registry,
   which no longer holds those changes, cannot list them, enforce them or
   tell when this is done. Its guarantee after a restore is what the backup
   held.
judgement.divergence: One implementation runs the missed daily backup immediately when the owner-only restored instance starts, preserving unreconciled data in a new backup; another suspends backups until the owner declares reconciliation complete. The owner and anyone relying on erasure reaching backups notice the different retained data and retention period.
judgement.why: The texts assign reconciliation to the owner and require a missed backup at startup, but do not say whether backup runs are suspended during reconciliation or identify a completion event for the scheduler.

topics.topic: Audit-number non-reuse when instance marks are lost during restore
questions: Is non-reuse after every restore an unconditional model invariant, or is restore after loss of the instance marks an explicit exception?
Is non-reuse after every restore an absolute model invariant, or only a guarantee when the instance marks survive and match the restored store?

quotes:
its sequence number, minted by Registry: greater than every number minted
  before it, starting at 1; never reused, also after old entries are erased
  (R0-66) or the store is restored (State 2 A15), so the log's order is the
  order of the numbers even where two entries share an instant (owner,
  2026-10-31; codex round-02 T2).

Marks that are missing are made from the
   store's last number, with a diagnostic: only a loss of the marks together
   with a restore could lower the numbering, and that is outside Registry's
   guarantees (A18 rule 10).
judgement.why: M09 unconditionally says numbers are never reused after restoration, while A15 expressly admits a restore after loss of the marks can lower the numbering.

topics.topic: Confirmation validity and consumption at the expiry boundary
questions: Is a confirmation submitted exactly 10 minutes after it was shown still valid, and does an expired but otherwise matching value consume the pending confirmation?
Is a confirmation submitted exactly 10 minutes after it was shown valid or expired?

quotes:
It is valid only in that session, for 10
   minutes, and is used up by the first submission that carries it, whatever
   its answer; a refused submission needs the step shown again.

A confirmation value used once — even by a refused submission — is refused
   the second time; one older than 10 minutes is refused.
judgement.divergence: One implementation accepts a matching confirmation exactly 10 minutes after it was shown; another treats it as expired and refuses it. The owner notices whether the confirmed action occurs at that boundary.
judgement.why: The text refuses values older than 10 minutes but does not define whether equality at exactly 10 minutes is valid.

topics.topic: Crash-safe atomic audit-sequence reservation and instance-mark updates
questions: What crash-safe protocol guarantees that a committed audit entry can never have a number higher than the durable instance mark, and that a torn mark cannot cause reuse?
Is reserving an audit sequence number an explicit exception to A04's all-or-none rule, or must the reservation be atomic with the change and therefore reusable after failure?

quotes: Every action is atomic: it applies all its changes or none.

Before such a change commits, Registry records its
   number in the instance marks — a small file in the backup location, apart
   from the store and the backups, which a restore does not replace (A18); a
   change that then fails leaves its number unused for ever, and the log
   skips it. At start Registry continues above the higher of the store's
   last number and the marks'. Marks that are missing are made from the
   store's last number, with a diagnostic: only a loss of the marks together
   with a restore could lower the numbering, and that is outside Registry's
   guarantees (A18 rule 10).

Instance marks that
   exist but cannot be read fail the start (A15).
judgement.divergence: One implementation durably and atomically replaces and synchronizes the instance mark before allowing the store transaction to commit; another merely writes or buffers it before commit, allowing a crash to leave a committed audit number above the durable mark or a torn mark. The owner notices reused or unavailable audit numbering after restart or restore.
judgement.why: The required ordering is stated, but the texts do not define the durability and crash-atomicity needed for the external mark to preserve the promised audit invariant.

topics.topic: Operation-specific service-token authority and required checks
questions: Do the operation rows in A09 override the generic trusted-service permissions in State 0, or must every service with the stated class receive those generic operations?
Are checks operation-dependent—one for registration, two for session-only operations and three for project operations—or must every agent-authority call undergo three checks?

quotes:
Every service token names one service; Registry knows from its own release
   which operations that service may call and the highest disclosure class it
   may receive (R0-26, R0-27). The configuration holds the tokens, not their
   rights (R0-20, R0-23).
An operation outside a token's row is refused, whatever the request holds.

A call with agent authority is accepted only when the token is Cabinet
   Kernel's, the session it names is registered, and — for an operation on a
   project — the project is in that session's set (R0-46, R0-53).
   'Register an agent session' is checked for the token only: the session it
   names is the one it registers (R0-53).
judgement.why: A09 makes authority operation-specific rather than class-wide, and A10 explicitly makes registration require only the token while adding session and project checks only where applicable.

topics.topic: Owner-session cookie attributes and scope
questions: What exact cookie attributes and host/path scope enforce the intended boundary, including access on the production host and HTTPS access from another machine?
What exact cookie scope and attributes enforce the intended boundary, especially when another service or port shares Registry's host?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about owner-session cookie scope and attributes, already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Owner-session cookie scope and attributes enforcing the browser/origin boundary
quotes: The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only to Registry's own origin.
precedent.why: Exact cookie attributes, host/path scope and SameSite transport policy are HTTP contract and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Owner-session validity required at commit time
questions: Can an owner request authenticated just before the absolute or idle deadline commit after the deadline, or must the session still be valid when the action commits?
If an owner request begins while the session is valid but the idle or eight-hour limit passes before its change commits, is the change accepted or refused?

quotes:
The session ends at the first of: 8 hours after sign-in; 30 minutes without
   an owner request; the owner's sign-out; the instance's restart (M11 is never
   durable). An owner request is any request to the owner interface that
   carries the valid session, whatever its answer; it restarts the 30
   minutes; before the first request it runs from the sign-in.

owner_session s valid at t <=> t < s.began + 8h and
                                t < s.last_request + 30min and
                                not signed_out(s) and no restart since s.began

Every operation — read or change, of a service, Kernel or the owner —
   checks in one order, and the first failure is its answer; a stage that
   does not apply to it is skipped, and each check an operation states belongs
   to the stage of its kind: (1) the caller's authentication and its right to
   the operation (A09) — for the owner, a valid owner session, then its CSRF
   value, then a confirmation value where one is asked (A13);
judgement.divergence: One implementation checks session validity when authenticating the request and permits the action to commit after the deadline; another rechecks at commit and refuses or rolls back it once the deadline passes. The owner notices whether the requested change is applied.
judgement.why: The texts define validity at an unspecified time t and the order of checks, but do not say whether validity must still hold when an owner action commits.
